text: Specification of the coding system for the CLHLS 1998-2018 longitudinal dataset (including the 1998 baseline survey, 2000, 2002, 2005, 2008, 2011, 2014, and 2018 follow-up surveys of both survivors and deceased persons)

This dataset is derived from the first eight waves (1998, 2000, 2002, 2005, 2008, 2011, 2014, and 2018) of the Chinese Longitudinal Healthy Longevity Survey (CLHLS). The CLHLS covers 23 out of 31 provinces in China. This dataset consists of fifteen components. The first component contains all the information collected in the 1998 baseline survey for 9,093 respondents. The second component contains information collected in the 2000 survey for 4,831 respondents who were re-interviewed in the 2000 survey. The third component includes information collected from the next-of-kin of 3,368 deceased persons who were first interviewed in 1998 but had died before the 2000 follow-up survey. The fourth component is for 2,643 respondents who were first interviewed in 1998 and re-interviewed in 2000 and 2002. The fifth component includes information obtained from the next-of-kin of 1,604 respondents who were first interviewed in 1998, survived at 2000 survey but died before 2002 survey. The sixth component is for the information collected in the 2005 survey for 1,051 respondents who were re-interviewed in 2000, 2002, and 2005. The seventh component contains information collected from the next-of-kin of 1,308 respondents who were interviewed in all previous three waves but died before the 2005 wave. The eighth component is for the information collected in the 2008 survey for 358 respondents who were re-interviewed in 2000, 2002, 2005, and 2008. The ninth component contains information collected from the next-of-kin of 480 respondents who were interviewed in 1998, survived at 2000, 2002, and 2005 survey but died before 2008 survey. The tenth component is for the information collected in the 2011 survey for 128 respondents who were re-interviewed in 2000, 2002, 2005, 2008, and 2011. The eleventh component contains information collected from the next-of-kin of 177 respondents who were interviewed in all previous five waves but died before the 2011 wave. The twelfth component is for the information collected in the 2014 survey for 47 respondents who were re-interviewed in 2000, 2002, 2005, 2008, 2011, 2014, and 2018. The thirteen component contains information collected from the next-of-kin of 75 respondents who were interviewed in all previous six waves but died before the 2014 survey. The 14th component contains information collected in the 2018 survey for 10 respondents who were interviewed in 2018. The 15th component includes information collected from the next-of-kin of 23 deceased persons who were interviewed in 2014 but had died before the 2018 follow-up survey. There were 894 respondents lost to follow-up in the 2000 survey, 585 respondents lost to follow-up in the 2002 survey, 284 respondents lost to follow in the 2005 survey, 214 respondents lost to follow in the 2008 survey, 53 respondents lost to follow in the 2011 survey, 6 respondents lost to follow in the 2014 survey, and 14 respondents lost to follow in the 2018 survey. This dataset is called the 1998-2018 longitudinal dataset. It presents both static and twenty-year interval dynamic information for the respondents who were first interviewed in 1998.

2. Variables and the coding system in this data set are based on questions in the individual questionnaire in the 1998 baseline survey, questions not in shaded boxes in the individual questionnaire in the 2000, 2002, 2005, 2008, 2011, 2014, and 2018 follow-up surveys, and questions in the questionnaire for the deceased person in the 2000, 2002, 2005, 2008, 2011, 2014, and 2018 follow-up surveys. The names of variables and the code system in this dataset, however, are not necessarily all the same as those in the corresponding questionnaires. Some are slightly different. Please use this coding system when performing analysis, and regard the questionnaire as a basic reference.

4. Most of variables are treated as ‘Numeric’ ones in this dataset, while some of them are treated as ‘string’ ones. Variables such as age, year, month, number of persons, and number of days are treated as ‘Scale’ type. Most of the remaining variables are treated as ‘Nominal’ ones including ‘yes’ or ‘no’ binomial questions. Variables in Part B, variables related to ADL, IADL functioning capacity in Part E, and some variables in Part D in the surviving individual questionnaires are treated as ‘Ordinal’ ones. ADL functioning before dying for the deceased persons are also treated as ‘Ordinal’ variables. More detailed information could be found in the ‘measurement level’ in the coding system.

6. Variables with names ‘_0’, ‘_2’, ‘_5’, ‘_8’, ‘_11’, ‘_14’, and ‘_18’ as their suffix are for those who were still alive and re-interviewed in 2000, 2002, 2005, 2008, 2011, 2014, and 2018 respectively, while variables with names ‘d0’, ‘d2’, ‘d5’, ‘d8’, ‘d11’, ‘d14’ and ‘d18’ as their prefix are variables for those deceased respondents who died in the survey intervals 1998-2000, 2000-2002, 2002-2005, 2005-2008, 2008-2011, 2011-2014, and 2014-2018 respectively.

9. ‘-6’ is used to indicate that the variable is used for surviving persons ONLY and is NOT applicable to the deceased persons. ‘-7’ is used to indicate that the variable is used for the deceased persons ONLY and is NOT applicable to the surviving respondents. ‘-8’ is used to indicate that the respondents were dead or lost to follow-up in an earlier wave, and ‘-9’ is used to define lost to follow-up. ‘–1’ is used in this dataset to indicate a situation in which the question is NOT applicable to the respondent. ‘9’, ‘99’, ‘999’, and ‘9999’ are usually used to represent missing information in different variables, while ‘8’, ‘88’, ‘888’, and ‘8888’ in most cases (but NOT all cases) are used to indicate situations in which the respondent didn’t know the answers to the questions. The missing values indicated by ‘8’, ‘88’, ‘888’, ‘8888’, ‘9’, ‘99’, ‘999’, and ‘9999’ need to be imputed by the user before doing the analysis, especially when the proportion of ‘missing’ or ‘don’t know’ is larger than 5%. Data sets with imputed values to replace the missing data are not currently available.

10. Nine variables in this dataset are non-survey variables. Eight of them (dth98_00, dth00_02, dth02_05, dth05_08, dth08_11, dth11_14, and dth14_18) indicate survival status in 2000, 2002, 2005, 2008, 2011, 2014, and 2018 surveys (i.e., surviving, dead, lost to follow-up). Another one (year9899) indicates the year of the interview of the baseline survey (Note: some of the samples were collected in 1999). The ninth variable is “w_1998” (see Note 13).
12. Attention should be given to time-varying variables. The information gathered in the 1998 baseline survey (e.g., number of marriages, information about the last marriage) is subject to change.

13. The weight variable “w_1998” is estimated based on the estimated numbers of oldest old persons by age, sex, and rural/urban residence in 1998 derived from 2000 census 100% data tabulations for the 22 provinces where the 1998 survey was conducted. The total number of the weighted individual cases of the survey is equal to the total sample size. However, the numbers of the weighted individual cases for the age-sex-residence-specific groups may not be exactly the same as the actual sub-sample size of the corresponding groups. Thus, SPSS, SAS, STATA (or other software) would not produce correct p-values for testing the statistical significance of the differences of the average proportions across different age-sex-reference groups, since the sub-sample size of the sub-groups may be altered after weighting the individual cases. Therefore, the weights need to be appropriately adjusted to ensure that the sub-sample size within each sub-group after weighting is exactly the same as the true sub-sample size for the cross sub-groups comparisons by using statistical significance tests. Such adjusted weights are available upon request. Please refer to Zeng and Vaupel et al. (2001: Appendix A) for details on how the weights and the adjusted weights are computed. Weight is not applied to those respondents aged less than 80 or more than 106 at their first interviews.

14. The eligible respondents of this dataset are those people aged 80 and over. There are a very few respondents in this data set whose age was less than 80 at the baseline survey, however. It’s recommended to exclude the respondents who were less than 80 years old if the analysis is focused on the oldest old since they had not reached the oldest old age (80+) at the survey time.

Specification of the coding system for the CLHLS 2000-2018 longitudinal dataset (including the 2000 baseline survey, 2002, 2005, 2008, 2011, 2014, and 2018 follow-up surveys of both survivors and deceased persons)

This dataset is derived from the first six waves (1998, 2000, 2002, 2005, 2008, 2011, 2014, and 2018) of the Chinese Longitudinal Healthy Longevity Survey (CLHLS). The CLHLS covers 23 out of 31 provinces in China. This dataset consists of thirteen components. The first component contains all the information collected in the 1998 baseline survey for 11,199 respondents. The second component contains information collected in the 2002 survey for 6,315 respondents who were re-interviewed in the 2002 survey. The third component includes information collected from the next-of-kin of 3,343 deceased persons who were first interviewed in 2000 but had died before the 2002 follow-up survey. The fourth component is for 2,628 respondents who were first interviewed in 2000 and re-interviewed in 2002 and 2005. The fifth component includes information obtained from the next-of-kin of 2,963 respondents who were first interviewed in 2000, survived at 2002 survey but died before 2005 survey. The sixth component is for the information collected in the 2008 survey for 950 respondents who were re-interviewed in 2002, 2005, and 2008. The seventh component contains information collected from the next-of-kin of 1,174 respondents who were interviewed in all previous three waves but died before the 2008 wave. The eighth component is for the information collected in the 2011 survey for 363 respondents who were re-interviewed in 2002, 2005, 2008, and 2011. The ninth component contains information collected from the next-of-kin of 458 respondents who were interviewed in 2002, survived at 2005, and 2008 survey but died before 20011 survey. The tenth component is for the information collected in the 2014 survey for 143 respondents who were re-interviewed in 2002, 2005, 2008, 2011, 2014, and 2018. The 11th component contains information collected from the next-of-kin of 201 respondents who were interviewed in all previous five waves but died before the 2014 wave. The 12th component contains information collected in the 2018 survey for 30 respondents who were interviewed in 2018. The 13th component includes information collected from the next-of-kin of 68 deceased persons who were interviewed in 2014 but had died before the 2018 follow-up survey. Out of 11,199 total respondents who were interviewed in 2000, there were 1,541 respondents lost to follow-up in the 2002 survey, 724 respondents lost to follow-up in the 2005 survey, 505 respondents lost to follow in the 2008 survey, 129 respondents lost to follow in the 2011 survey, 19 respondents lost to follow in the 2014 survey, and 45 respondents lost to follow in the 2018 survey. This dataset is called the 2000-2018 longitudinal dataset. It presents both static and eighteen-year interval dynamic information for the respondents who were first interviewed in 2000.

2. Variables and the coding system in this data set are based on questions in the individual questionnaire in the 2000 baseline survey, questions not in shaded boxes in the individual questionnaire in the 2002, 2005, 2008, 2011, 2014, and 2018 follow-up surveys, and questions in the questionnaire for the deceased person in the 2002, 2005, 2008, 2011, 2014, and 2018 follow-up surveys. The names of variables and the code system in this dataset, however, are not necessarily all the same as those in the corresponding questionnaires. Some are slightly different. Please use this coding system when performing analysis, and regard the questionnaire as a basic reference.

4. Most of variables are treated as ‘Numeric’ ones in this dataset, while some of them are treated as ‘string’ ones. Variables such as age, year, month, number of persons, and number of days are treated as ‘Scale’ type. Most of the remaining variables are treated as ‘Nominal’ ones including ‘yes’ or ‘no’ binomial questions. Variables in Part B, variables related to ADL, IADL functioning capacity in Part E, and some variables in Part D in the surviving individual questionnaires are treated as ‘Ordinal’ ones. ADL functioning before dying for the deceased persons are also treated as ‘Ordinal’ variables. More detailed information could be found in the ‘measurement level’ in the coding system.

6. Variables with names ‘_2’, ‘_5’, ‘_8’, ‘_11’, ‘_14’, and ‘_18’ as their suffix are for those who were still alive and re-interviewed in 2002, 2005, 2008, 2011, 2014, and 2018 respectively, while variables with names ‘d2’, ‘d5’, ‘d8’, ‘d11’, ‘d14’, and ‘d18’ as their prefix are variables for those deceased respondents who died in the survey intervals 2000-2002, 2002-2005, 2005-2008, 2008-2011, 2011-2014, and 2014-2018, respectively.

7. ‘-6’ is used to indicate that the variable is used for surviving persons ONLY and is NOT applicable to the deceased persons. ‘-7’ is used to indicate that the variable is used for the deceased persons ONLY and is NOT applicable to the surviving respondents. ‘-8’ is used to indicate that the respondents were dead or lost to follow-up in an earlier wave, and ‘-9’ is used to define lost to follow-up. ‘–1’ is used in this dataset to indicate a situation in which the question is NOT applicable to the respondent. ‘9’, ‘99’, ‘999’, and ‘9999’ are usually used to represent missing information in different variables, while ‘8’, ‘88’, ‘888’, and ‘8888’ in most cases (but NOT all cases) are used to indicate situations in which the respondent didn’t know the answers to the questions. The missing values indicated by ‘8’, ‘88’, ‘888’, ‘8888’, ‘9’, ‘99’, ‘999’, and ‘9999’ need to be imputed by the user before doing the analysis, especially when the proportion of ‘missing’ or ‘don’t know’ is larger than 5%. Data sets with imputed values to replace the missing data are not currently available.

8. Seven variables in this dataset are non-survey variables. Six of them (dth00_02, dth02_05, dth05_08, dth08_11, dth11_14, and dth14_18) indicate survival status in 2002, 2005, 2008, 2011, 2014, and 2018 surveys (i.e., surviving, dead, lost to follow-up). The seventh variable is “w_2000” (see Note 11).
10. Attention should be given to time-varying variables. The information gathered in the 1998 baseline survey (e.g., number of marriages, information about the last marriage) is subject to change.

11. The weight variable “w_2000” is estimated based on the numbers of oldest old persons by age, sex, and rural/urban residence in 2000 from 2000 census 100% data tabulations for the 22 provinces where the 2000 survey was conducted. The total number of the weighted individual cases of the survey is equal to the total sample size. However, the numbers of the weighted individual cases for the age-sex-residence-specific groups may not be exactly the same as the actual sub-sample size of the corresponding groups. Thus, SPSS, SAS, STATA (or other software) would not produce correct p-values for testing the statistical significance of the differences of the average proportions across different age-sex-reference groups, since the sub-sample size of the sub-groups may be altered after weighting the individual cases. Therefore, the weights need to be appropriately adjusted to ensure that the sub-sample size within each sub-group after weighting is exactly the same as the true sub-sample size for the cross sub-groups comparisons by using statistical significance tests. Such adjusted weights are available upon request. Please refer to Zeng and Vaupel et al. (2001: Appendix A) for details on how the weights and the adjusted weights are computed. Weight is not applied to those respondents aged less than 80 or more than 106 at their first interviews.

12. The eligible respondents of this dataset are those people aged 80 and over. There are a very few respondents in this data set whose age was less than 80 at the baseline survey, however. It’s recommended to exclude the respondents who were less than 80 years old if the analysis is focused on the oldest old since they had not reached the oldest old age (80+) at the survey time.

Specification of the coding system for the CLHLS 2002-2018 longitudinal dataset (including the 2002, 2005, 2008, 2011, 2014, and 2018 waves of both survivors and deceased persons)

This dataset is derived from the 2002, 2005, 2008, 2011, 2014, and 2018 waves of the Chinese Longitudinal Healthy Longevity Survey (CLHLS). The CLHLS covers 23 out of 31 provinces in China. This dataset consists of eleven components. The first component contains all the information collected in the 2002 survey for 16,064 respondents who were interviewed in 2002. The second component contains information collected in the 2005 survey for 8,175 respondents who were re-interviewed in 2005 (i.e., follow-up survivors). The third component includes information collected from the next-of-kin of 5,874 deceased persons who were interviewed in 2002 but had died before the 2005 follow-up survey. The fourth component is the information collected in 2008 for 4,191 respondents who were still alive at the time of the 2008 survey. The fifth component is the information obtained from the next-of-kin of 2,520 respondents who were interviewed in 2002, re-interviewed in 2005, but died before the 2008 survey. The sixth component is the information collected in 2011 for 2,513 respondents who were still alive at the time of the 2011 survey. The seventh component is the information obtained from the next-of-kin of 1,184 respondents who were interviewed in 2002, re-interviewed in 2005 and 2008, but died before the 2011 survey. The eighth component is the information collected in 2014 for 1,681 respondents who were still alive at the time of the 2014 survey. The ninth component is the information obtained from the next-of-kin of 717 respondents who were interviewed in 2002, re-interviewed in 2005, 2008, and 2011, but died before the 2014 survey. A very small part of respondents were interviewed for twice in the 2011 wave, one in 2011 and another in 2012 for more in-depth study. Among the 1,184 deceased samples in 2011, 1 was interviewed in the 2011 survey as survivors during 2008-2011 and died before the 2012 more in-depth survey. The 10th component contains information collected in the 2018 survey for 790 respondents who were interviewed in 2018. The 11th component includes information collected from the next-of-kin of 484 deceased persons who were interviewed in 2014 but had died before the 2018 follow-up survey. Out of 16,064 total respondents who were interviewed in 2002, 2,015 respondents were lost to follow-up in the 2005 survey, 1,464 respondents were lost to follow-up in 2008, 494 respondents were lost to follow-up in 2011, 116 respondents were lost to follow-up in 2014, and 408 respondents were lost to follow-up in 2018. This dataset is called the 2002-2018 longitudinal data. It presents both static and sixteen-year interval dynamic information for the respondents interviewed in 2002.

2. Variables and the coding system in this data set are based on questions from the individual questionnaire in the 2002 survey, questions not in shaded boxes in the individual questionnaire in the 2005, 2008, 2011, 2014, and 2018 follow-up surveys, and questions in the questionnaire for deceased person in the 2005, 2008, 2011, 2014, and 2018 follow-up surveys. The names of variables and the code system in this dataset, however, are not necessarily all the same as those in the corresponding questionnaires. Some are slightly different. Please use this coding system when performing analysis, and take the questionnaire as a basic reference.

4. Most of variables are treated as ‘Numeric’ ones in this dataset, while some of them are treated as ‘string’ ones. Variables such as age, year, month, number of persons, and number of days are treated as ‘Scale’ type. Most of the remaining variables are treated as ‘Nominal’ ones including ‘yes’ or ‘no’ binomial questions. Variables in Part B, variables related to ADL, IADL functioning capacity in Part E, and some variables in Part D in the surviving individual questionnaires are treated as ‘Ordinal’ ones. ADL functioning before dying for the deceased persons are also treated as ‘Ordinal’ variables. More detailed information could be found in the ‘measurement level’ in the coding system.

6. Variables with names ‘_5’, ‘_8’, ‘_11’, ‘_14’, and ‘_18’ as their suffix are for those who were still alive and re-interviewed in 2005, 2008, 2011, 2014, and 2018, respectively, while variables with names ‘d5’, ‘d8’, ‘d11’, ‘d14’, and ‘d18’ as their prefix are variables for those deceased respondents who died in the survey intervals of 2002-2005, 2005-2008, 2008-2011, 2011-2014, and 2014-2018, respectively.

7. ‘-6’ is used to indicate that the variable is used for surviving persons ONLY and is NOT applicable to the deceased persons. ‘-7’ is used to indicate that the variable is used for the deceased persons ONLY and is NOT applicable to the surviving respondents. ‘-8’ is used to indicate that the respondents were dead or lost to follow-up in an earlier wave, and ‘-9’ is used to define lost to follow-up. ‘–1’ is used in this data set to indicate a situation in which the question is NOT applicable to the respondent. ‘9’, ‘99’, ‘999’, and ‘9999’ are usually used to represent missing information in different variables, while ‘8’, ‘88’, ‘888’, and ‘8888’ in most cases (but NOT all cases) are used to indicate situations in which the respondent didn’t know the answers to the questions. The missing values indicated by ‘8’, ‘88’, ‘888’, ‘8888’, ‘9’, ‘99’, ‘999’, and ‘9999’ need to be imputed by the user before doing the analysis, especially when the proportion of ‘missing’ or ‘don’t know’ is larger than 5%. The data sets with imputed values to replace the missing data are not currently available.

8. There are six variables (i.e. dth02_05, dth05_08, dth08_11, dth11_14, dth14_18, and w_2002) in this dataset that are non-survey variables. The variables of “dth02_05”, “dth05_08”, “dth08_11”, “dth11_14”, and “dth14_18”, indicate survival status in the 2005, 2008, 2011, 2014, and 2018 surveys (i.e., surviving, dead, lost to follow-up). The sixth variable is “w_2002” (see Note 11).
9. Attention should be given to time-varying variables. The information gathered in the 2002 survey (e.g., number of marriages, information about the last marriage) is subject to change.

11. The weight variable “w_2002” is estimated based on the numbers of elderly persons by age, sex, and rural/urban residence in 2002 from 2000 census 100% data tabulations for the 22 provinces where the 2000 survey was conducted. The total number of the weighted individual cases of the survey is equal to the total sample size. However, the numbers of the weighted individual cases for the age-sex-residence-specific groups may not be exactly the same as the actual sub-sample size of the corresponding groups. Thus, SPSS, SAS, STATA (or other software) would not produce correct p-values for testing the statistical significance of the differences of the average proportions across different age-sex-reference groups, since the sub-sample size of the sub-groups may be altered after weighting the individual cases. Therefore, the weights need to be appropriately adjusted to ensure that the sub-sample size within each sub-group after weighting is exactly the same as the true sub-sample size for the cross sub-groups comparisons by using statistical significance tests. Such adjusted weights are available upon request. Please refer to Zeng and Vaupel et al. (2001: Appendix A) for details on how the weights and the adjusted weights are computed. Weight is not applied to those respondents aged less than 65 or more than 106 at their first interviews.

12. The eligible respondents in this data set are those people aged 80 and over. There are very few respondents in this data set whose age was less than 80 at the baseline survey, however. It’s recommended to exclude the respondents who were less than 80 years old if the analysis is focused on the oldest old since they had not reached the oldest old age (80+) at the survey time.

Specification of the coding system for the CLHLS 2005-2018 longitudinal dataset (including the 2005, 2008, 2011, 2014, and 2018 waves of both survivors and deceased persons)

This dataset is derived from the 2005, 2008, 2011, 2014 and 2018 waves of the Chinese Longitudinal Healthy Longevity Survey (CLHLS). The CLHLS covers 23 out of 31 provinces in China. This dataset consists of nine components. The first component contains all the information collected in the 2005 survey for 15,638 respondents who were interviewed in 2005. The second component contains information collected in the 2008 survey for 7,472 respondents who were re-interviewed in 2008 (i.e., follow-up survivors). The third component includes information collected from the next-of-kin of 5,228 deceased persons who were interviewed in 2005 but had died before the 2008 follow-up survey. The fourth component is the information collected in 2011 for 4,191 respondents who were still alive at the time of the 2011 survey. The fifth component is the information obtained from the next-of-kin of 2,255 respondents who were interviewed in 2005, re-interviewed in 2008, but died before the 2011 survey. The sixth component is the information collected in 2014 for 2,791 respondents who were still alive at the time of the 2014 survey. The seventh component is the information obtained from the next-of-kin of 1,185 respondents who were interviewed in 2005, re-interviewed in 2008 and 2011, but died before the 2014 survey. A very small part of respondents were interviewed for twice in the 2011 wave, one in 2011 and another in 2012 for more in-depth study. Among the 2,255 deceased samples in 2011, 1 was interviewed in the 2011 survey as survivors during 2008-2011 and died before the 2012 more in-depth survey. The eighth component contains information collected in the 2018 survey for 1,330 respondents who were interviewed in 2018. The ninth component includes information collected from the next-of-kin of 760 deceased persons who were interviewed in 2014 but had died before the 2018 follow-up survey. Out of 15,638 total respondents who were interviewed in 2005, 2,938 respondents were lost to follow-up in the 2008 survey, 1,026 respondents were lost to follow-up in 2011, 216 respondents were lost to follow-up in 2014, and 702 respondents were lost to follow-up in 2018. This dataset is called the 2005-2018 longitudinal data. It presents both static and 13-year interval dynamic information for the respondents interviewed in 2005.

2. Variables and the coding system in this data set are based on questions in the individual questionnaire in the 2005 survey, questions not in shaded boxes in the individual questionnaire in the 2008, 2011, 2014, and 2018 follow-up surveys, and questions in the questionnaire for the deceased person in the 2008, 2011, 2014, and 2018 follow-up surveys. The names of variables and the code system in this dataset, however, are not necessarily all the same as those in the corresponding questionnaires. Some are slightly different. Please use this coding system when performing analysis, and take the questionnaire as a basic reference.

4. Most of variables are treated as ‘Numeric’ ones in this dataset, while some of them are treated as ‘string’ ones. Variables such as age, year, month, number of persons, and number of days are treated as ‘Scale’ type. Most of the remaining variables are treated as ‘Nominal’ ones including ‘yes’ or ‘no’ binomial questions. Variables in Part B, variables related to ADL, IADL functioning capacity in Part E, and some variables in Part D in the surviving individual questionnaires are treated as ‘Ordinal’ ones. ADL functioning before dying for the deceased persons are also treated as ‘Ordinal’ variables. More detailed information could be found in the ‘measurement level’ in the coding system.

6. Variables with names ‘_8’, ‘_11’, ‘_14’, and ‘_18’ as their suffix are for those who were still alive and re-interviewed in 2008, 2011, 2014, and 2018, respectively, while variables with names ‘d8’, ‘d11’, ‘d14’, and ‘d18’ as their prefix are variables for those deceased respondents who died in the survey intervals of 2005-2008, 2008-2011, 2011-2014, and 2014-2018, respectively.

7. ‘-6’ is used to indicate that the variable is used for surviving persons ONLY and is NOT applicable to the deceased persons. ‘-7’ is used to indicate that the variable is used for the deceased persons ONLY and is NOT applicable to the surviving respondents. ‘-8’ is used to indicate that the respondents were dead or lost to follow-up in an earlier wave, and ‘-9’ is used to define lost to follow-up. ‘–1’ is used in this data set to indicate a situation in which the question is NOT applicable to the respondent. ‘9’, ‘99’, ‘999’, and ‘9999’ are usually used to represent missing information in different variables, while ‘8’, ‘88’, ‘888’, and ‘8888’ in most cases (but NOT all cases) are used to indicate situations in which the respondent didn’t know the answers to the questions. The missing values indicated by ‘8’, ‘88’, ‘888’, ‘8888’, ‘9’, ‘99’, ‘999’, and ‘9999’ need to be imputed by the user before doing the analysis, especially when the proportion of ‘missing’ or ‘don’t know’ is larger than 5%. 11. The weight variable “w_2005” is estimated based on the numbers of elderly persons by age, sex, and rural/urban residence in 2005 from the 2000 census 100% data tabulations for the 22 provinces where the 2005 survey was conducted. The total number of the weighted individual cases of the survey is equal to the total sample size. However, the numbers of the weighted individual cases for the age-sex-residence-specific groups may not be exactly the same as the actual sub-sample size of the corresponding groups. Thus, SPSS, SAS, STATA (or other software) would not produce correct p-values for testing the statistical significance of the differences of the average proportions across different age-sex-reference groups, since the sub-sample size of the sub-groups may be altered after weighting the individual cases. Therefore, the weights need to be appropriately adjusted to ensure that the sub-sample size within each sub-group after weighting is exactly the same as the true sub-sample size for the cross sub-groups comparisons by using statistical significance tests. Such adjusted weights are available upon request. Please refer to Zeng and Vaupel et al. (2001: Appendix A) for details on how the weights and the adjusted weights are computed. Weight is not applied to those respondents aged less than 65 or more than 106 at their first interviews.

Specification of the coding system for the CLHLS 2008-2018 longitudinal dataset (including the 2008, 2011, 2014, and 2018 waves of both survivors and deceased persons)

This dataset is derived from the 2008, 2011, 2014, and 2018 waves of the Chinese Longitudinal Healthy Longevity Survey (CLHLS). The CLHLS covers 23 out of 31 provinces in China. This dataset consists of seven components. The first component contains all the information collected in the 2008 survey for 16,954 respondents who were interviewed in 2008. The second component contains information collected in the 2011 survey for 8,418 respondents who were re-interviewed in 2011. The third component includes information collected from the next-of-kin of 5,642 deceased persons who were interviewed in 2008 but had died before the 2011 follow-up survey. The fourth component is the information collected in 2014 for 5,245 respondents who were still alive at the time of the 2014 survey. The fifth component is the information obtained from the next-of-kin of 2,589 respondents who were interviewed in 2008, re-interviewed in 2011, but died before the 2014 survey. A very small part of respondents were interviewed for twice in the 2011 wave, one in 2011 and another in 2012 for more in-depth study. Among the 5,642 deceased samples, 7 were interviewed in the 2011 survey as survivors during 2008-2011 and died before the 2012 more in-depth survey. The six component contains information collected in the 2018 survey for 2,440 respondents who were interviewed in 2018. The seven component includes information collected from the next-of-kin of 1,547 deceased persons who were interviewed in 2014 but had died before the 2018 follow-up survey. Out of 16,954 total respondents who were interviewed in 2008, 2,894 respondents were lost to follow-up in the 2011 survey, d 591 respondents were lost to follow-up in the 2014 survey, and 1,259 respondents were lost to follow-up in the 2018 survey. This dataset is called the 2008-2018 longitudinal data. It presents both static and ten-year interval dynamic information for the respondents interviewed in 2008.

2. Variables and the code system in this data set are based on questions in the individual questionnaire in the 2008 survey, questions not in shaded boxes in the individual questionnaire in the 2011, 2014 and 2018 follow-up survey, and questions in the questionnaire for the deceased person in the 2011, 2014 and 2018 follow-up survey. The names of variables and the code system in this dataset, however, are not necessarily all the same as those in the corresponding questionnaires. Some are slightly different. Please use this coding system when performing analysis, and take the questionnaire as a basic reference.

4. Most of variables are treated as ‘Numeric’ ones in this dataset, while some of them are treated as ‘string’ ones. Variables such as age, year, month, number of persons, and number of days are treated as ‘Scale’ type. Most of the remaining variables are treated as ‘Nominal’ ones including ‘yes’ or ‘no’ binomial questions. Variables in Part B, variables related to ADL, IADL functioning capacity in Part E, and some variables in Part D in the surviving individual questionnaires are treated as ‘Ordinal’ ones. ADL functioning before dying for the deceased persons are also treated as ‘Ordinal’ variables. More detailed information could be found in the ‘measurement level’ in the coding system.

6. Variables with names ‘_11’, ‘_14’ and ‘_18’ as their suffix are for those who were still alive and re-interviewed in 2011, 2014 and 2018, respectively, while variables with names ‘d11’, ‘d14’ and ‘d18’ as their prefix are variables for those deceased respondents who died in the survey interval of 2008-2011, 2011-2014 and 2014-2018, respectively.

7. ‘-6’ is used to indicate that the variable is used for surviving persons ONLY and is NOT applicable to the deceased persons. ‘-7’ is used to indicate that the variable is used for the deceased persons ONLY and is NOT applicable to the surviving respondents, and ‘-9’ is used to define lost to follow-up. ‘–1’ is used in this data set to indicate a situation in which the question is NOT applicable to the respondent. ‘9’, ‘99’, ‘999’, and ‘9999’ are usually used to represent missing information in different variables, while ‘8’, ‘88’, ‘888’, and ‘8888’ in most cases (but NOT all cases) are used to indicate situations in which the respondent didn’t know the answers to the questions. The missing values indicated by ‘8’, ‘88’, ‘888’, ‘8888’, ‘9’, ‘99’, ‘999’, and ‘9999’ need to be imputed by the user before doing the analysis, especially when the proportion of ‘missing’ or ‘don’t know’ is larger than 5%. The data sets with imputed values to replace the missing data are not currently available.

8. There are four variables (i.e., dth08_11, dth11_14, dth14_18 and w_2008) in this dataset are non-survey variables. The variable of “dth08_11”, “dth11_14” and “dth14_18” indicate survival status in the 2011, 2014 and 2018 surveys (i.e., surviving, dead, lost to follow-up). Another variable is “w_2008” (see Note 11).
9. Attention should be given to time-varying variables. The information gathered in the 2008 survey (e.g., number of marriages, information about the last marriage) is subject to change.

11. The weight variable “w_2008” is estimated based on the numbers of elderly persons by age, sex, and rural/urban residence in 2008 from the 2010 census 100% data tabulations for the 23 provinces where the 2008 survey was conducted. The total number of the weighted individual cases of the survey is equal to the total sample size. However, the numbers of the weighted individual cases for the age-sex-residence-specific groups may not be exactly the same as the actual sub-sample size of the corresponding groups. Thus, SPSS, SAS, STATA (or other software) would not produce correct p-values for testing the statistical significance of the differences of the average proportions across different age-sex-reference groups, since the sub-sample size of the sub-groups may be altered after weighting the individual cases. Therefore, the weights need to be appropriately adjusted to ensure that the sub-sample size within each sub-group after weighting is exactly the same as the true sub-sample size for the cross sub-groups comparisons by using statistical significance tests. Such adjusted weights are available upon request. Please refer to Zeng and Vaupel et al. (2001: Appendix A) for details on how the weights and the adjusted weights are computed. Weight is not applied to those respondents aged less than 65 or more than 106 at their first interviews.

12. The eligible respondents in this data set are those people aged 65 and over. There are a very few respondents in this data set whose age was less than 65 at the baseline survey, however. It’s recommended to exclude the respondents who were less than 65 years.

Specification of the coding system for the CLHLS 2011-2018 longitudinal dataset (including the 2011/2012, 2014 and 2018 waves of both survivors and deceased persons)

This dataset is derived from the 2011/2012, 2014 and 2018 waves of the Chinese Longitudinal Healthy Longevity Survey (CLHLS). The CLHLS covers 23 out of 31 provinces in China. This dataset consists of five components. The first component contains all the information collected in the 2011/2012 survey for 9,765 respondents who were interviewed in 2011/2012. The second component contains information collected in the 2014 survey for 6,066 respondents who were interviewed in 2014. The third component includes information collected from the next-of-kin of 2,879 deceased persons who were interviewed in 2011/2012 but had died before the 2014 follow-up survey. The four component contains information collected in the 2018 survey for 2,884 respondents who were interviewed in 2018. The five component includes information collected from the next-of-kin of 1,837 deceased persons who were interviewed in 2014 but had died before the 2018 follow-up survey. Out of 9,765 total respondents who were interviewed in 2011/2012, 820 respondents were lost to follow-up in the 2014 survey, and 1,345 respondents were lost to follow-up in the 2018 survey. This dataset is called the 2011-2018 longitudinal data. It presents both static and seven-year interval dynamic information for the respondents interviewed in 2011/2012.

2. Variables and the code system in this data set are based on questions in the individual questionnaire in the 2011/2012 survey, questions not in shaded boxes in the individual questionnaire in the 2014 and 2018 follow-up surveys, and questions in the questionnaire for the deceased person in the 2014 and 2018 follow-up surveys. The names of variables and the code system in this dataset, however, are not necessarily all the same as those in the corresponding questionnaires. Some are slightly different. Please use this coding system when performing analysis, and take the questionnaire as a basic reference.

4. Most of variables are treated as ‘Numeric’ ones in this dataset, while some of them are treated as ‘string’ ones. Variables such as age, year, month, number of persons, and number of days are treated as ‘Scale’ type. Most of the remaining variables are treated as ‘Nominal’ ones including ‘yes’ or ‘no’ binomial questions. Variables in Part B, variables related to ADL, IADL functioning capacity in Part E, and some variables in Part D in the surviving individual questionnaires are treated as ‘Ordinal’ ones. ADL functioning before dying for the deceased persons are also treated as ‘Ordinal’ variables. More detailed information could be found in the ‘measurement level’ in the coding system.

6. Variables with names ‘_14’ and ‘_18’ as their suffix are for those who were still alive and re-interviewed in 2014 and 2018, respectively, while variables with names ‘d14’ and ‘d18’ as their prefix are variables for those deceased respondents who died in the survey interval of 2011-2014 and 2014-2018.

7. ‘-6’ is used to indicate that the variable is used for surviving persons ONLY and is NOT applicable to the deceased persons. ‘-7’ is used to indicate that the variable is used for the deceased persons ONLY and is NOT applicable to the surviving respondents, and ‘-9’ is used to define lost to follow-up. ‘–1’ is used in this data set to indicate a situation in which the question is NOT applicable to the respondent. ‘9’, ‘99’, ‘999’, and ‘9999’ are usually used to represent missing information in different variables, while ‘8’, ‘88’, ‘888’, and ‘8888’ in most cases (but NOT all cases) are used to indicate situations in which the respondent didn’t know the answers to the questions. The missing values indicated by ‘8’, ‘88’, ‘888’, ‘8888’, ‘9’, ‘99’, ‘999’, and ‘9999’ need to be imputed by the user before doing the analysis, especially when the proportion of ‘missing’ or ‘don’t know’ is larger than 5%. The data sets with imputed values to replace the missing data are not currently available.

8. There are three variables (i.e., dth11_14, dth14_18 and w_2011) in this dataset are non-survey variables. The variable of “dth11_14” and “dth14_18” indicates survival status in the 2014 and 2018 surveys (i.e., surviving, deceased, lost to follow-up). Another variable is “w_2011” (see Note 11).
9. Attention should be given to time-varying variables. The information gathered in the 2011 survey (e.g., number of marriages, information about the last marriage) is subject to change.

11. The weight variable “w_2011” is estimated based on the estimated numbers of elderly persons by age, sex, and rural/urban residence in 2011 derived from the 6th census conducted in 2010 for the 22 provinces where the 2011 follow-up survey was conducted. The total number of the weighted individual cases of the survey is equal to the total sample size. However, the numbers of the weighted individual cases for the age-sex-residence-specific groups may not be exactly the same as the actual sub-sample size of the corresponding groups. Thus, SPSS, SAS, STATA (or other software) would not produce correct p-values for testing the statistical significance of the differences of the average proportions across different age-sex-reference groups, since the sub-sample size of the sub-groups may be altered after weighting the individual cases. Therefore, the weights need to be appropriately adjusted to ensure that the sub-sample size within each sub-group after weighting is exactly the same as the true sub-sample size for the cross sub-groups comparisons with statistical significant test. Such adjusted weights are available upon request. Please refer to Zeng and Vaupel et al. (2001: Appendix A) for details on how the weights and the adjusted weights are computed. Specification of the coding system for the CLHLS 2014-2018 longitudinal dataset (including the 2014 and 2018 waves of both survivors and deceased persons)

This dataset is derived from the 2014 and 2018 waves of the Chinese Longitudinal Healthy Longevity Survey (CLHLS). The CLHLS covers 23 out of 31 provinces in China. This dataset consists of three components. The first component contains all the information collected in the 2014 survey for 7,192 respondents who were interviewed in 2014. The second component contains information collected in the 2018 survey for 3,441 respondents who were interviewed in 2014. The third component includes information collected from the next-of-kin of 2,226 deceased persons who were interviewed in 2014 but had died before the 2018 follow-up survey. Out of 7,192 total respondents who were interviewed in 2014, 1,525 respondents were lost to follow-up in the 2018 survey. This dataset is called the 2014-2018 longitudinal data. It presents both static and three-year interval dynamic information for the respondents interviewed in 2014.

2. Variables and the code system in this data set are based on questions in the individual questionnaire in the 2014 survey, questions not in shaded boxes in the individual questionnaire in the 2018 follow-up survey, and questions in the questionnaire for the deceased person in the 2018 follow-up survey. The names of variables and the code system in this dataset, however, are not necessarily all the same as those in the corresponding questionnaires. Some are slightly different. Please use this coding system when performing analysis, and take the questionnaire as a basic reference.

4. Most of variables are treated as ‘Numeric’ ones in this dataset, while some of them are treated as ‘string’ ones. Variables such as age, year, month, number of persons, and number of days are treated as ‘Scale’ type. Most of the remaining variables are treated as ‘Nominal’ ones including ‘yes’ or ‘no’ binomial questions. Variables in Part B, variables related to ADL, IADL functioning capacity in Part E, and some variables in Part D in the surviving individual questionnaires are treated as ‘Ordinal’ ones. ADL functioning before dying for the deceased persons are also treated as ‘Ordinal’ variables. More detailed information could be found in the ‘measurement level’ in the coding system.

6. Variables with names ‘_18’ as their suffix are for those who were still alive and re-interviewed in 2018, while variables with names ‘d18’ as their prefix are variables for those deceased respondents who died in the survey interval of 2014-2018.

7. ‘-6’ is used to indicate that the variable is used for surviving persons ONLY and is NOT applicable to the deceased persons. ‘-7’ is used to indicate that the variable is used for the deceased persons ONLY and is NOT applicable to the surviving respondents, and ‘-9’ is used to define lost to follow-up. ‘–1’ is used in this data set to indicate a situation in which the question is NOT applicable to the respondent. ‘9’, ‘99’, ‘999’, and ‘9999’ are usually used to represent missing information in different variables, while ‘8’, ‘88’, ‘888’, and ‘8888’ in most cases (but NOT all cases) are used to indicate situations in which the respondent didn’t know the answers to the questions. The missing values indicated by ‘8’, ‘88’, ‘888’, ‘8888’, ‘9’, ‘99’, ‘999’, and ‘9999’ need to be imputed by the user before doing the analysis, especially when the proportion of ‘missing’ or ‘don’t know’ is larger than 5%. The data sets with imputed values to replace the missing data are not currently available.

8. There are two variables (i.e., dth14_18, and w_2014) in this dataset are non-survey variables. The variable of “dth14_18” indicates survival status in the 2018 surveys (i.e., surviving, deceased, lost to follow-up). Another variable is “w_2014” (see Note 11).
9. Attention should be given to time-varying variables. The information gathered in the 2014 survey (e.g., number of marriages, information about the last marriage) is subject to change.

11. The weight variable “w_2014” is estimated based on the estimated numbers of elderly persons by age, sex, and rural/urban residence in 2014 derived from the 6th census conducted in 2010 for the 22 provinces where the 2014 follow-up survey was conducted. The total number of the weighted individual cases of the survey is equal to the total sample size. However, the numbers of the weighted individual cases for the age-sex-residence-specific groups may not be exactly the same as the actual sub-sample size of the corresponding groups. Thus, SPSS, SAS, STATA (or other software) would not produce correct p-values for testing the statistical significance of the differences of the average proportions across different age-sex-reference groups, since the sub-sample size of the sub-groups may be altered after weighting the individual cases. Therefore, the weights need to be appropriately adjusted to ensure that the sub-sample size within each sub-group after weighting is exactly the same as the true sub-sample size for the cross sub-groups comparisons with statistical significant test. Such adjusted weights are available upon request. Please refer to Zeng and Vaupel et al. (2001: Appendix A) for details on how the weights and the adjusted weights are computed. Weight is not applied to those respondents aged less than 65 or more than 106 at their first interviews.

12. The eligible respondents in this data set are those people aged 65 and over. There are a very few respondents in this data set whose age was less than 65 at the baseline survey, however. It’s recommended to exclude the respondents who were less than 65 years.

Specifications of the coding system for the CLHLS 2018 wave cross-sectional dataset of elderly aged 65+

1. This dataset is derived from the seventh wave of the Chinese Longitudinal Healthy Longevity Survey (CLHLS) in 2018. The CLHLS covers 23 out of 31 provinces in China. The 2018 follow-up survey contains 15,874 respondents aged 65+; and 10 of them were interviewed in all seven waves in 1998, 2000, 2002, 2005, 2008, 2011/2012, and 2014; 30 of them were interviewed in 2000, 2002, 2005, 2008/2009, 2011/2012, and 2014; 790 were interviewed in 2002, 2005, 2008/2009, 2011/2012 and 2014; 1,330 were interviewed in 2005, 2008/2009, 2011/2012 and 2014; 2,440 were interviewed in 2008/2009, 2011/2012 and 2014; 2,884 were interviewed in2011/2012 and 2014; 3,463 were interviewed in 2014 only; and 12,411 of them were newly interviewed in 2018.

4. This is the released Version 1.0 for the 2018 cross-sectional dataset. The ID in this released version has eight digits, which is generated from the national provincial code, questionnaire No., and the last two digits of the year of the very first interview of the interviewee.

5. Most of variables are treated as ‘Numeric’ones in this dataset, while some of them are treated as ‘string’ ones. ‘Scale’variables such as age, year, month, number of persons, and number of days are treated as ‘Scale’ type. Most of the remaining ‘Numeric’variables are treated as ‘Nominal’ ones including ‘yes’ or ‘no’ binominal questions. Variables in Part B, variables related to ADL, IADL functioning capacity in Part E, and some variables in Part D in the surviving individual questionnaires are treated as ‘Ordinal’ ones. More detailed information could be found in the ‘measurement level’ in the coding system.

8. The weight variable “w_2018” is estimated based on the estimated numbers of elderly persons by age, sex, and rural/urban residence in 2018 derived from the 1% random sampling mini-census conducted in 2015 for the 23 provinces where the 2018 follow-up survey was conducted. The total number of the weighted individual cases of the survey is equal to the total sample size. However, the numbers of the weighted individual cases for the age-sex-residence-specific groups may not be exactly the same as the actual sub-sample size of the corresponding groups. Thus, SPSS, SAS, STATA (or other software) would not produce correct p-values for testing the statistical significance of the differences of the average proportions across different age-sex-reference groups, since the sub-sample size of the sub-groups may be altered after weighting the individual cases. Therefore, the weights need to be appropriately adjusted to ensure that the sub-sample size within each sub-group after weighting is exactly the same as the true sub-sample size for the cross sub-groups comparisons with statistical significant test. Such adjusted weights are available upon request. Please refer to Zeng and Vaupel et al. (2001: Appendix A) for details on how the weights and the adjusted weights are computed. Weight is not applied to those respondents aged less than 65 or more than 106 at their first interviews. The weight variable is located at the end of the dataset.
